Article Title: Mahela Jayawardene likely to continue as Mumbai Indians coach; status quo on trade chatter
Article Text:
Mahela Jayawardene (left) and Hardik Pandya

Don't be surprised if he [Hardik Pandya] is not traded at all. Discussions have also happened with the player along these lines. For a trade to happen, multiple things need to fall into place. So it's not that straightforward. Sources

Hardik Pandya

NEW DELHI: Former Sri Lanka captain Mahela Jayawardene is likely to continue as Mumbai Indians (MI) head coach for the 2027 edition of the Indian Premier League (IPL), with the franchise reluctant to make sweeping changes. It is learnt that Jayawardene joined the five-time champions on a "two + one" contract in 2024 and could well be given another year, considering it will be the last year of the ongoing cycle. A formal announcement is expected next month, provided there is no late change of heart.Under Jayawardene, Mumbai Indians reached the playoffs in 2025 but finished ninth the following year. 2026 was a disappointing season for the IPL giants, as they won only four games in a campaign marred by injuries, availability concerns and unrest in the dressing room.Since the disappointing last season, there has been a lot of chatter around their captain Hardik Pandya's potential trade. While multiple franchises have expressed interest, there has yet to be any substantial movement on that front.TimesofIndia.com has also learnt that some dialogue has taken place with the Kolkata Knight Riders (KKR), but the lack of a tradeable asset has not excited MI at the moment. Cameron Green's name was on the table, but the MI think tank is wary of the Australian's workload next year, which includes Australia's packed Test calendar.As far as the Chennai Super Kings (CSK) are concerned, some action is expected once they finalise their new head coach.How will MI tackle the Pandya situation? They are keen on retaining him as a player for the upcoming season as they plan to head in a new direction under a new captain. The management has already explored this idea, and it is learnt that former India and MI captain Rohit Sharma is actively involved in discussions about the captaincy and the team's direction. Returning Rohit to the captaincy was also an option, but a new face is likely as the 39-year-old is not keen to wear the armband again. Tilak Varma and Jasprit Bumrah are two potential options, with the scales tilting in the former's favour."Don't be surprised if he is not traded at all. Discussions have also happened with the player along these lines. For a trade to happen, multiple things need to fall into place. So it's not that straightforward," says a source tracking developments.It will be interesting to see how the dynamics unfold if Pandya is not traded at all and how the franchise addresses the dressing room unrest. A change in captaincy is something they expect will restore normalcy, but navigating the turbulence will require significant effort. Another matter that will need attention is that of recently sacked India T20I captain Suryakumar Yadav . Apart from Pandya, there was chatter around the T20 specialist, but the franchise seems in no mood to let go of their experienced campaigner."Yes, he didn't have a good season last year, but what about the ones before that? MI will not discard a player based on one season, and that's not how they operate. They take pride in the 'One Family' tag and swear by it," adds the source.As things stand, continuity has been the bottom line. While a reset cannot be ruled out from the next cycle, there is no desperation for the 2027 edition. A captaincy change is inevitable, but it may not be a surprise if the status quo continues on other matters.
Article Summary: Mahela Jayawardene is likely to continue as Mumbai Indians head coach for the 2027 edition of the Indian Premier League (IPL) The franchise are reluctant to make sweeping changes. A formal announcement is expected next month, provided there is no late change of heart. There has been a lot of chatter around Hardik Pandya's potential trade.

Article Text:

NEW DELHI: At the recently concluded BWF World Championships , players weighed every word as carefully as their drop shots. But beyond the glare of the cameras, another contest was quietly unfolding. Standing a step behind the athletes were the interpreters, almost invisible yet carrying the immense responsibility of ensuring that nuance survived the journey from Mandarin, Japanese or Korean into English.At a World Championships, where every word can travel as quickly as a smash, a mistranslated phrase can soften conviction, distort the meaning of an entire exchange or, in the worst case, trigger an unintended geopolitical controversy. For the interpreters, getting the words right is only part of the job. The real challenge is ensuring that nothing gets lost in translation.Chaavi Raj, one of the three Mandarin interpreters, felt the pressure immediately when local hope Ayush Shetty stunned World No. 1 and defending champion Shi Yu Qi in the opening round."There was a lot of pressure. There were so many media houses present. My first match was with Ayush Shetty. China lost. It was a big upset," explained the third-year PhD student in Chinese Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University.For the 29-year-old Raj, it was a daunting first assignment. He had worked for businesses, exhibitions, tourists and ministries. Sports and media were new territory.Raj, who hails from Bihar's Sitamarhi district, has been studying the Chinese language for five years and travelled to Beijing for a visiting scholarship. After his first preference, Spanish, did not materialise, he shifted his focus to Mandarin, graduating in Chinese Language and Culture Studies."Like India, where there are multiple dialects, Chinese also changes with region, context and tone. It was difficult in the beginning. It is a pictographic language. You have to memorise it. This is the challenge of Mandarin," he explained."It is a tonal language. If the tone changes, the meaning changes. It is very easy to forget. It is difficult to memorise. We watch videos to keep ourselves in touch. We watch web series and movies. We talk to our Chinese friends. We do all this to stay in touch with the language," he added.The BWF brought three interpreters of its own to the tournament, while the Badminton Association of India (BAI) recruited three more through a PR firm and a third-party vendor.Sahin Parween and Nandini were two of the other interpreters roped in by the BAI. Parween, a recent graduate from JNU's School of Language, Literature and Culture Studies, was first intrigued by Japanese culture while watching animated series such as Doraemon and Shin-chan. Her interest was reinforced later in life as anime found its feet in India. The fact that Japanese is a high-paying language in India has also played a role, she admits almost sheepishly."We are paid between Rs 4,000 and Rs 10,000 per day. Korean and Japanese generally pay better if you compare them with Western languages. The rate can even go up to $200 (Rs 19,000) or more," says Parween, who graduated just a month ago.Like Parween, Nandini's route to Korean was similarly shaped by pop culture. After picking up the language in 2018, her interest was piqued by K-pop and K-dramas. Perhaps unsurprisingly, language was already part of her life: her father speaks 13 Indian languages.Still relatively new to the profession, the duo spent days training ahead of the World Championships, which returned to India after a gap of 17 years."When we found out the tournament was happening, we searched what it was about. Then we searched for the vocabulary and the questions the media could ask. Then we prepared for what the players could reply to those questions. Still, there was some nervousness," explained Nandini, who is a third-year BA student of Korean Language and Culture.Before the World Championships assignment, they would chip in when ambassadors or exchange students visited JNU. Both also make the most of opportunities to meet Japanese, Korean and Chinese people as part of university discussions.This, however, was a different challenge altogether."There is a lot of pressure when you know that the player is relying on you solely. When the question is asked, they look at our faces, and it's up to us. And we have to explain it in the right way," says Nandini.For the youngsters, the pressure was complicated by another fact: they were often interpreting for players they admired."At the same time, we are also their fans. We just blank out sometimes because we are very busy processing, okay, 'we are seeing them in real life'. Also, it happens in interpretation that when something is asked or said, we may know the word but we just blank out because of nervousness. So, we find another way to say it," she said."There are times when we feel like we could have done better. We have moments where we are unsure of the most appropriate word. But at the end of the day, we are also learning," she continued.Choosing the right word can be the difference between a routine interview and a diplomatic incident. During the Cold War, disputed translations of Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev's remarks and a notorious mistranslation of US President Jimmy Carter's 1977 speech in Poland became famous examples of how a few misplaced words can distort meaning.Mandarin interpreter Chaavi Raj understands the importance of every word in his preparations. His PhD studies focus on China-US relations and the perception of former American diplomat and Secretary of State Henry Kissinger. He prepares by studying archival footage of the players' previous interviews. Increasingly, AI tools have become part of that preparation."We see the videos beforehand, the interviews they have given in Chinese. Then we prepare the words. We see which words can be used well. We also take the help of AI. We give prompts asking the tool to go through the videos and suggest which words and vocabulary are repeated most often. Sometimes we write it down, sometimes we make notes," Raj explains his process."It is very important to do it right. In such a big event, where there can be a diplomatic incident, you cannot take a chance," he says while showcasing his notebook full of Chinese characters, or Hanzi.By the time the last microphone is lowered and the player disappears towards the lounge, the interpreters have already faded into the background. Their names rarely make the broadcast or the byline, yet every headline, quote and television soundbite owes something to their precision. In a sport decided by millimetres, theirs is another game of fine margins: finding the right word, preserving the meaning and making sure nothing gets lost between the player and the world.
Article Summary: The 30th edition of the BWF World Championships 2026 took place from August 17 to August 23 at the Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium in New Delhi, India. For the interpreters, getting the words right is only part of the job. The real challenge is ensuring that nothing gets lost in translation.

Article Title: ‘Pakistan cricket has hit a panic button’: Ramiz Raja slams PCB over unprecedented England tour overhaul
Article Text:
Pakistan cricket team (ANI Photo)

Ramiz questions unprecedented overhaul

Changes come amid Lord’s controversy

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Former Pakistan batter and PCB chairman Ramiz Raja has criticised the current board for what he described as a panic-driven response to the team’s disastrous Test tour of England.The PCB made sweeping changes after Pakistan lost the first two Tests of the three-match series, sending seven players home before the final match in Birmingham. Mohammad Rizwan, Imam-ul-Haq and Salman Ali Agha are among those dropped from the tour, while seven replacements have been brought into the squad.The changes have also extended to the coaching staff. Head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and assistant coach Umar Gul have been released from their positions, with white-ball coach Mike Hesson set to take charge for the third Test.Ramiz believes the scale and timing of the overhaul could further damage the confidence of the Pakistan players rather than solve the team’s problems.“I'm trying to convince myself this is all OK, but it is not. It just shows Pakistan cricket has hit a panic button. It's not good for the game, it's not good for the confidence of the players who have come in, or for the players who are left, because it makes you a selfish team,” Ramiz, BBC Radio 5 Live.“What is the guarantee they will get the results? Some of these guys have not played Test cricket. I've got no idea why this was done,” he added.Pakistan’s performances in England have been poor from the outset.They suffered an innings defeat in the opening Test at Headingley before England won the Lord’s Test by 194 runs. Across their four innings in the series, Pakistan have failed to reach 200 on every occasion.However, Ramiz questioned whether replacing such a large number of players midway through a tour could suddenly change the team’s fortunes.“I'm really not happy with the situation. How many times have we seen this happen in world cricket? Never, ever. This is more like football, midway through the season, firing a manager. If you ask me how things can be fixed, I've got no idea,” said Ramiz.The former PCB chairman also pointed to the uncertainty created for both the players being sent home and those suddenly brought into the squad.With the third Test fast approaching, several newcomers will be expected to adapt quickly to Test cricket and the conditions in England.The PCB’s drastic decisions have come during an already turbulent tour.The Lord’s Test was played against the backdrop of an off-field dispute involving the sons of former Pakistan captain and prime minister Imran Khan.Sky Sports broadcast an interview with Suleiman and Kasim Khan during the lunch interval on the opening day. The programme focused on their father’s circumstances and prompted reports that the PCB had considered withdrawing Pakistan from the remainder of the Test and potentially the tour.Pakistan ultimately continued playing, while captain Babar Azam and head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed said they were unaware of any plan to boycott the match.The timing of the latest changes has also attracted attention because the Pakistan squad is scheduled to meet King Charles at Clarence House during its stay in the UK.Pakistan will now attempt to salvage something from the tour when they face England in the third and final Test in Birmingham.
Article Summary: Ramiz questions unprecedented overhaul of Pakistan's cricket team. Seven players have been sent home and seven replacements brought in. Head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and assistant coach Umar Gul have been released from their positions, with white-ball coach Mike Hesson set to take charge for the third Test.

Article Title: Carlos Alcaraz makes winning US Open return after wrist injury: ‘I had more nerves than usual’
Article Text:
Carlos Alcaraz, of Spain, celebrates winning a match against Roman Safiullin, of Russia, during the first round of the U.S. Open tennis championships, Monday, Aug. 31, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo/Sydney Schaefer)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Sabalenka starts title defence

Carlos Alcaraz made a winning return to Grand Slam tennis at the US Open on Monday, and the biggest positive was that his injured right wrist felt completely fine.The 23-year-old Spaniard beat Roman Safiullin 6-4, 6-4, 6-4 despite missing the French Open and Wimbledon since April.“I don’t know how it looked from outside, but from inside, my feeling was that I was hitting normal,” Alcaraz said. “I was playing pretty normal, playing my style, and yeah, the arm, the wrist, everything felt great.”Alcaraz admitted he was more nervous than usual because he had not played a Grand Slam match for several months. Still, he said his main aim was to enjoy the tournament and see how his body responds.“I had more nerves than usual, but just happy, because, for me, my goal here is to compete, to enjoy, and let’s see how my body’s going to react after the matches, after the competition again,” Alcaraz said.“I don’t know how far I’m going to go in the tournament. I didn’t know if I was going to lose this one, if I’m going to make the second round, final. I don’t know how far I’m going to go. But what I just really want to do is enjoy every time that I’m going to walk into the court feeling the energy from the people, feel the competition.”His chances of defending the title have received a boost after Novak Djokovic suffered a shock first-round defeat, while top-ranked Jannik Sinner is sidelined with a knee injury.Two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka also began strongly, beating Camila Osorio 6-4, 6-4. She is aiming to become the first player since Serena Williams to win three straight US Open titles.“I feel like this is one of my favorite stadiums,” Sabalenka told the crowd afterward. “I really experienced the best emotions here in this stadium.”Meanwhile, Stefanos Tsitsipas eliminated 10th seed Arthur Fils and was asked whether he could rediscover his best form.“Why not?” Tsitsipas said.
Article Summary: Carlos Alcaraz makes winning return to Grand Slam tennis at US Open. Spaniard beat Roman Safiullin despite missing French Open and Wimbledon. Two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka also began strongly. Stefanos Tsitsipas eliminated 10th seed Arthur Fils.

Article Title: Rohit Rajpal throws hat into ring for AITA president’s post
Article Text:
DLTA president Rohit Rajpal announces candidature for All India Tennis Association presidency

New Delhi:

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Rohit Rajpal has thrown his hat into the ring for the All India Tennis Association (AITA) president’s post, setting up a potentially keen contest ahead of elections likely to be held in late Oct or early Nov this year.The AITA is currently functioning under the interim supervision of court-appointed administrator, retired Justice Gita Mittal. The administrator has opened the process for Sportsperson of Outstanding Merit (SOM) candidates seeking to contest the elections for AITA office-bearer posts.Rajpal, 55, will contest through the general body and file his nomination through his state association. He is currently president of the Delhi Lawn Tennis Association (DLTA), an Executive Committee member of the Indian Olympic Association (IOA), an AITA office-bearer and the non-playing captain of the Indian Davis Cup team.“It is after a lot of introspection and interactions with well-wishers in the tennis fraternity and other friends that I have decided to contest the forthcoming elections of the prestigious All India Tennis Association as President,” Rajpal said in a statement.“Tennis is not just a sport for me; it has been my life since the time I was a young boy who wished to make it big. At 55, when many summers have passed, my heart still beats for Indian tennis.It is my dream and vision for India that a sport which has produced so many champions at home should grow further by leaps and bounds,” he added.Rajpal, a former Asian Junior champion and Asian Games medallist whose playing career was cut short by a serious back injury, said his experience in tennis administration and the Davis Cup had strengthened his resolve to seek the top post.“Having been involved in tennis matters at large for almost a decade in AITA and DLTA has been a learning and enriching hands-on experience,” he said. “As the non-playing Davis Cup captain of Team India in several Davis Cup engagements, it was enormously satisfying to be with and motivate our immensely talented players to give their best and bring glory to the nation by advancing to the second-round qualifiers.”India will face South Korea in Seoul on September 18-19 for a place in the final eight of the Davis Cup. Rajpal, however, will have to relinquish the Davis Cup captaincy if he is elected AITA president.“This journey has given me the confidence to now step forward and announce my candidature as President of All India Tennis Association as a step forward in my desire to contribute to the growth and development of tennis in India,” Rajpal said.“With your support, I plan to adopt player-centric approach and policies, good governance and transparency above all. I plan to share my vision document in due course,” he added.Chintan Parikh of the Gujarat association is also expected to contest the president’s post. It is learnt that Indian tennis legend and Bengal Tennis Association president Leander Paes could also enter the fray. Paes, who took charge of the Bengal association in Nov 2025, would likely come through the SOM route and file his nomination.
Article Summary: Rohit Rajpal has thrown his hat into the ring for the All India Tennis Association (AITA) president’s post. Rajpal, 55, will contest through the general body and file his nomination through his state association. Bengal Tennis Association president Leander Paes could also enter the fray.

Article Title: Siddhesh Lad to replace Shardul Thakur as Mumbai captain for 2026-27 Ranji Trophy season
Article Text:
Siddhesh Lad and Shardul Thakur (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Mumbai: Mumbai will have a new captain for the second successive Ranji Trophy season, with seasoned batter Siddhesh Lad set to take charge of the 42-time champions in the 2026-27 campaign. Lad will replace allrounder Shardul Thakur , who led Mumbai across formats during the previous domestic season.Confirming the development, Mumbai senior selection committee chairman Rajesh Pawar said the decision was taken keeping both leadership continuity and workload management in mind.“Yes, we’ve decided to appoint Siddhesh as our captain for the 2026-27 Ranji Trophy season. He did well last season and is experienced. Shardul is our match-winner. There is already too much workload on him as he’s expected to bowl a lot of overs, take wickets and contribute with the bat as well. We don’t want to burden him with the responsibility of captaincy. Plus, we’ll have to manage his workload. There are 10 games in the Ranji Trophy and he may have to rest for the odd match,” Pawar told TOI on Monday.Pawar said both players had been consulted before the move was finalised.“We’ve spoken to both Siddhesh and Shardul about it, and both are positive about it. Since the season starts with four Ranji Trophy matches in October, we wanted clarity on the captaincy well in advance,” he added.The appointment rewards a stellar domestic season from Lad, who was Mumbai’s standout performer with the bat in the 2025-26 Ranji Trophy. The 34-year-old amassed 774 runs in eight matches at an impressive average of 77.40, striking five centuries to finish as the team’s leading run-scorer.Over the course of an accomplished first-class career, Lad has compiled 5,623 runs in 82 matches at 44.27, including 15 hundreds and 30 fifties. Mumbai begin their Ranji Trophy season against Chandigarh at Wankhede Stadium from Oct 11-14. They are placed in Elite Group D alongside Chandigarh, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Rajasthan, Railways, Tamil Nadu and Uttarakhand. Mumbai last lifted the Ranji Trophy in 2023-2024 under Ajinkya Rahane.
Article Summary: Siddhesh Lad will captain Mumbai in the 2026-27 Ranji Trophy season. The 34-year-old replaces Shardul Thakur, who led Mumbai across formats last season. Mumbai begin their campaign against Chandigarh at Wankhede Stadium from Oct 11-14.

Article Title: ‘Nothing went according to my plans’: K Humpy opens up ahead of Olympiad title defence
Article Text:
K Humpy

TOI

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

K Humpy, India’s top-ranked woman chess player, was unwilling to state her preferred board number for Team India at the Olympiad. Nor did she say that she would play according to the wishes of the team or captain. But she dropped enough hints.“I have played a few Olympiads and have always played on board one. For many years, we have been following the rating procedure for maintaining the board order. I don’t know how they are going to look at it this year,” Humpy toldfrom Vijayawada on Monday. Top seeds India are set to defend their gold medal in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, starting Sept 16.Humpy finished eighth with 3.5 points in the nine-round classical Cairns Cup in St Louis, USA. But her Norway Chess campaign in May-June, where she finished sixth and last, was particularly disappointing. “It’s not so comfortable to enter into the Olympiad in such a scenario,” said Humpy. “I'm just waiting to get back in good shape. I was a bit rusty but it happens to every player. You’ll be in that bad phase and then you’ll come out of it.On her poor run in Norway, Humpy said, “I played the tournament after a very long gap.Nothing went according to my plans. This year was disturbing. I was also a bit upset with the off-the-board things and probably that also reflected in the way I played.”Humpy withdrew from the Candidates tournament in Cyprus after FIDE turned down her request to shift the eight-player women’s world championship qualifier to a safer venue, citing security concerns arising from the war in West Asia.“I think I’m fine now,” she said. “Probably, it did disturb me for a few months. Like, it’s not easy for a player who has been professional and working towards it and then taking all the negativity. So it did affect me. I spent many sleepless nights as well. But for the last month or so, I have been in better shape.”
Article Summary: K Humpy, India’s top-ranked woman chess player, was unwilling to state her preferred board number for Team India at the Olympiad. Top seeds India are set to defend their gold medal in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, starting Sept 16.

Article Title: 'Good for nothing': Danish Kaneria lambasts Pakistan cricket, calls it 'a shame after 70 years'
Article Text:
Players greet each other at the end of the play on day four of the second cricket test match between England and Pakistan in London, Sunday, Aug. 30, 2026. (AP Photo/Dave Shopland)

Kaneria questions Pakistan’s team and bowling attack

Call for major changes in domestic cricket

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Former Pakistan spinner Danish Kaneria has strongly criticised the country’s cricket system after Pakistan suffered a 0-2 Test series defeat against England. He questioned the team’s selection, coaching, domestic cricket structure and the lack of accountability within the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB).Pakistan’s 194-run loss at Lord’s gave England an unassailable lead in the series. In response, Pakistan released seven players from the squad and removed head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and bowling coach Umar Gul. But Kaneria believes changing personnel will not solve the deeper problems.Kaneria said Pakistan’s cricket has lost its competitiveness and the fighting spirit that was once associated with the team. He also criticised the repeated changes in leadership and selection.“It's a shame that after 70 years, Pakistan has gone through such a disaster. There is no logic, selection committee, or play. They are just good for nothing. You see, such a bad performance. If a person loses, he tries and fights before losing. The fight has to be visible. Here, there’s no fight. No one knows anything,” he told news agency IANS.He also questioned why coaches and selectors are appointed for short periods before being removed, saying the system needs stability and people who are willing to take responsibility for both wins and losses.Kaneria was particularly unhappy with Pakistan’s bowling options. He pointed out that experienced players such as Mohammad Abbas, who took nine wickets at Lord’s, and spinner Noman Ali have been overlooked despite performing well.“And the bowling attack is pathetic. Who is Muhammad Shahzad? Where did he come from? He doesn’t have any line or length. No swing, no reverse swing. Nothing.”He also criticised Pakistan’s batting approach in English conditions, particularly the dismissals of Babar Azam and Mohammad Rizwan.“Like a player of the calibre of Babar Azam is getting out like this. This is pathetic. And then you are keeping Rizwan for so long. I don't know what he is doing. Why is he even there?”Kaneria believes the problems begin well before players reach the national team. He blamed the weakening of domestic cricket and the closure of departmental cricket for reducing the quality of Pakistan’s talent pool.“I like how the BCCI have put in their contracts that first class cricket is important. At least you play 5 to 6 games. None of our boys play domestic. And this downfall of Pakistan cricket started when the structure of domestic cricket changed.”He argued that selectors need to regularly watch domestic matches instead of relying heavily on performances in the Pakistan Super League.“The reason is that the talent pool has been eliminated. There is no doubt there’s talent pool in Pakistan but this selection happens mostly based on PSL.”Kaneria called for a strong selection committee, an experienced coach and a settled group of players who are given enough time to develop.“There are only a few players around whom Pakistan cricket revolves. There is no improvement. Need a strong coach and a strong selection committee.”Above all, he wants Pakistan to regain its competitive spirit.“We also used to lose. But fight and lose. At least fight. Fight, try at least! But there is no effort.”
Article Summary: Former Pakistan spinner Danish Kaneria has strongly criticised the country’s cricket system after Pakistan suffered a 0-2 Test series defeat against England. He questioned the team’S selection, coaching, domestic cricket structure and the lack of accountability within the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB)

Article Title: Big Blow for South Africa! Kagiso Rabada likely to miss Australia Test series with Hamstring Injury
Article Text:
Kagiso Rabada likely to miss Australia Tests (Image: Agency)

Donald confirms Rabada absence

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Proteas face pace-bowling concerns

South Africa are likely to suffer a major blow ahead of their three-match Test series against Australia, with premier fast bowler Kagiso Rabada ruled out after sustaining a severe Grade 3 tear in his right hamstring.The injury, picked up during Rabada’s winter conditioning programme, is expected to keep him out for up to 10 weeks, ruling him out of the high-profile series that begins in Durban on October 9.Former South Africa fast bowler and current Lions bowling coach Allan Donald confirmed that Rabada will miss the entire series, ending hopes of having him available for the domestic season.“He’s going to be out for all the Aussie Tests as well,” Donald was quoted as saying by South African media outlet News24 on Sunday.South Africa are scheduled to face Australia in three Tests, with the second match in Gqeberha from October 18 and the final Test in Cape Town from October 27. The series will be preceded by a three-match ODI series beginning in Durban on September 24.Rabada’s absence leaves a significant void in the South African bowling attack. Gerald Coetzee Corbin Bosch and youngster Kwena Maphaka are likely to shoulder greater responsibility in his absence. South Africa are also monitoring the fitness of Nandre Burger, who is recovering from a stress fracture in his back.However, there is still a chance that the left-arm pacer could recover in time to feature in the Test series.Meanwhile, Rabada has taken 340 wickets in 73 Tests and played a key role in South Africa’s victory over Australia in the 2025 World Test Championship final at Lord’s, where he finished with match figures of 9-110. He also boasts an impressive record against Australia, having claimed 58 wickets in 11 Tests at an average of 21.39.
Article Summary: Kagiso Rabada ruled out for up to 10 weeks with hamstring injury. South Africa face Australia in three-match Test series starting in Durban on October 9. Rabada has taken 340 wickets in 73 Tests and played a key role in South Africa's victory over Australia in the 2025 World Test Championship final at Lord's.

Article Title: ‘Pakistan was ruined that day’: Ex-cricketer blames Babar Azam-Shaheen Afridi rift for team’s downfall
Article Text:
Pakistan's Shaheen Shah Afridi, left. celebrates with teammate Babar Azam (AP Photo)

Babar and Shaheen captaincy saga

Former Pakistan batter Basit Ali has claimed that a fallout between Babar Azam and Shaheen Shah Afridi over the captaincy played a major role in the national team’s decline.Basit’s comments came after Pakistan’s miserable showing in England, where they have already surrendered the three-match Test series 2-0 following a 194-run defeat at Lord’s. The visitors have faced widespread criticism for their performances, with the team struggling to show any fight in either of the opening two Tests.According to Basit, however, Pakistan’s problems go much deeper than the current results. He believes the leadership dispute between two of the country’s senior players created a damaging divide within the setup.“Babar Azam is not a strong captain. I am not speaking about this based on the performance in England. He has made many wrong decisions. The main reason for Pakistan cricket's downfall is the rift between Shaheen and Babar. When there was a falling-out between the two over the captaincy, Pakistan cricket was ruined that day,” Ali said on the ‘Game Plan’ show.He also suggested that the consequences of the dispute are still visible in Pakistan cricket.“Many statements were made, saying Shaheen is a very good bowler and Babar is a very good bowler.The rift, whoever created that, the side effects can be seen now,” he added.Pakistan’s leadership has gone through repeated changes since the 2023 ODI World Cup.Babar stepped down as captain after Pakistan’s disappointing campaign in India, with Shaheen subsequently handed the ODI leadership. However, after Pakistan’s poor results in New Zealand, Babar returned to the captaincy.His second stint did not last long either. Babar was removed again after Pakistan failed to reach the semi-finals of the 2024 T20 World Cup.The constant reshuffling has now left Pakistan with separate captains across formats. Babar leads the Test side, Shaheen is the ODI captain, while Salman Ali Agha is in charge of the T20I team.Basit believes the damage caused by the earlier captaincy dispute cannot be ignored while assessing Pakistan’s current struggles.The PCB has now begun making changes following the disastrous England tour.On Monday, the board decided to send seven players home, with Mohammad Rizwan and Salman Ali Agha among those affected. Test coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and bowling coach Umar Gul were also removed from the setup.White-ball coach Mike Hesson will take charge of Pakistan for the third and final Test against England in Birmingham.While Babar remains Pakistan’s Test captain, Shaheen has not been part of the red-ball setup and is currently out of favour in Test cricket.Babar took over as Test captain from Shan Masood earlier this year. Under his leadership, Pakistan drew a two-match Test series against the West Indies.However, his own batting form in the longest format remains a concern. Babar has gone four years without scoring a Test century, adding to the pressure surrounding his leadership as Pakistan prepare for the final Test at Edgbaston.
Article Summary: Basit Ali believes the rift between Babar Azam and Shaheen Shah Afridi over the captaincy played a major role in the national team's decline. Pakistan have already surrendered the three-match Test series 2-0 following a 194-run defeat at Lord’s. The PCB has begun making changes following the disastrous England tour.

Article Title: ‘Not a good decision’: Ex-Pakistan cricketer fumes at PCB, sends message to Mohsin Naqvi
Article Text:

Former Pakistan cricketer Kamran Akmal has criticised the Pakistan Cricket Board's decision to release seven players from the squad midway through the England Test series, arguing that the move could have a damaging impact on the remaining members of the team.The PCB confirmed on Monday evening that Mohammad Rizwan , Salman Ali Agha and Imam-ul-Haq were among the seven players sent back to Pakistan after the team's disappointing results in the first two Tests against England.The board also announced seven replacements ahead of the third and final Test in Birmingham. In another major shake-up, Test head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and bowling coach Umar Gul were released from their roles, with white-ball coaches Mike Hesson and Ashley Noffke taking over.Akmal questioned the need to send senior players home when they could simply have been left out of the playing XI.“There was one more Test left. You could have had both Agha and Rizwan in the squad. You could have dropped them from the playing XI. You should have kept them in the squad. They are your senior players. They have been captains. Sending them back is not a good message for the remaining players,” Akmal said on the ‘Game Plan’ show.The former wicketkeeper-batter believes the decision could increase the pressure on those still in the squad, particularly with Pakistan already struggling during the series.“This will result in more pressure for the remainder of the team. It is not a good decision; if you are sending them back, then the chairman, Mohsin Naqvi, needs to rejig the entire system. Make a new team. This decision to send back players is not good for our country, and it doesn't send a good message to the rest of the world,” he added.Agha's situation has also raised questions over the timing of the decision. He captained Pakistan in the opening Test at Headingley in Babar Azam's absence but was subsequently dropped when the regular captain returned for the Lord's Test.Rizwan, meanwhile, endured a difficult series with the bat. He managed only 61 runs across his four innings against England and was also criticised for his shot selection and lack of game awareness.Imam's situation was different. After struggling in the opening Test, the opener picked up a calf injury while fielding on the first day of the second Test. He did not come out to bat afterwards, leading to questions over the seriousness of the injury. The controversy intensified when a former Pakistan selector later alleged that Imam had previously faked injuries.
Article Summary: Kamran Akmal has criticised the Pakistan Cricket Board's decision to release seven players from the squad midway through the England Test series. Mohammad Rizwan, Salman Ali Agha and Imam-ul-Haq were among the seven players sent back to Pakistan after the team's disappointing results in the first two Tests against England. The board also announced seven replacements ahead of the third and final Test in Birmingham.

Article Title: Major shake-up in Pakistan cricket after Lord’s rout: Seven players, coaches Sarfaraz, Gul released

Sarfaraz Ahmed, Umar Gul also released

Updated Pakistan Test squad for Birmingham Test: Babar Azam (captain), Abdullah Fazal, Arafat Minhas, Azan Awais, Mohammad Abbas, Mohammad Ali, Muhammad Imran, Mohammad Imran Jnr, Muhammad Ghazi Ghori (wicket-keeper), Razaullah, Saad Baig (wicket-keeper), Saim Ayub, Sajid Khan, Saud Shakeel, Shan Masood and Ubaid Shah

Pakistan have responded to their crushing 194-run defeat to England at Lord’s with a sweeping mid-tour overhaul, releasing seven players and making changes to the red-ball coaching staff ahead of the third Test at Edgbaston.The Pakistan Cricket Board announced the changes on Monday after Pakistan slipped to a 0-2 deficit in the three-match series. The defeat at Lord’s followed an innings-and-103-run loss in Leeds, leaving Pakistan with five defeats in their last six Tests.Among the seven players released are former white-ball captain Salman Ali Agha, wicketkeeper-batter Mohammad Rizwan and opening batter Imam-ul-Haq. Ali Usman, Aamir Jamal, Muhammad Awais Zafar and Khurram Shahzad have also been released.“The Pakistan Cricket Board has today announced that seven players have been released from the Test squad following completion of the Lord’s Test. A total of seven replacements have been named including five uncapped players at Test level and two capped players,” the PCB said in its statement.The board has brought in seven replacements, including Test-capped batters Saim Ayub and Abdullah Fazal, along with left-arm spin-bowling all-rounder Arafat Minhas.Saim has played eight Tests for Pakistan, while Abdullah has featured in two. Minhas has represented Pakistan in three ODIs and four T20Is.“Among the players announced as replacements, batters Saim Ayub and Abdullah Fazal have played eight and two Tests, respectively, while left-arm spin-bowling all-rounder Arafat Minhas has represented Pakistan in three ODIs and four T20Is,” the PCB said.Four uncapped players at Test level have also been added to the squad — left-arm fast bowler Mohammad Imran Jnr, wicketkeeper-batter Saad Baig, and right-arm pace-bowling all-rounders Mohammad Imran, also known as Imran Randhawa, and Razaullah.“The four other players are left-arm fast bowler Mohammad Imran Jnr, wicketkeeper-batter and player of the tournament of Quaid-e-Azam Trophy 2025-26 Saad Baig, right-arm pace bowling all-rounders Mohammad Imran (also known as Imran Randhawa) and Razaullah,” the PCB added.The changes extend beyond the playing squad, with red-ball head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and bowling coach Umar Gul also relieved of their duties.White-ball head coach Mike Hesson and Ashley Noffke will take over the backroom responsibilities for the remainder of the England tour.“Additionally, Sarfaraz Ahmed and Umar Gul have also been released and will be replaced by Mike Hesson and Ashley Noffke in the backroom staff,” the PCB said.The overhaul follows growing scrutiny of several players after the Lord’s defeat. Imam came under criticism after missing both innings because of a calf injury sustained on the opening day. His appearance on the outfield for warm-ups on the fourth morning drew further attention.Rizwan’s position had also come under pressure after another difficult outing with the bat. His dismissal in the second innings, when he was trapped lbw attempting a slog, added to questions over his place.Pakistan will now attempt to salvage something from the series when they face England in the third Test at Edgbaston from September 9.
Article Summary: Pakistan have responded to their crushing 194-run defeat to England at Lord’s with a sweeping mid-tour overhaul, releasing seven players and making changes to the red-ball coaching staff. The Pakistan Cricket Board announced the changes on Monday after Pakistan slipped to a 0-2 deficit in the three-match series. Red- ball head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and bowling coach Umar Gul also relieved of their duties.

Article Title: Zimbabwe survive huge Namibia scare, clinch five-run win in final-over thriller
Article Text:
Zimbabwe players (Pic credit: ICC)

Zimbabwe recover from 101/6

Namibia’s stunning fightback falls agonisingly short

Poll Vote & Share your view Which aspect of this match was the most thrilling for you? Last over drama Zimbabwe's initial collapse Namibia's stunning comeback Excellent individual performances 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Zimbabwe survived a stunning late fightback from Namibia to pull off a thrilling five-run victory in Windhoek, recovering from a precarious 101/6 to post 195/6 before holding their nerve in a dramatic final over.Namibia, who had opened the tri-series with an impressive win over South Africa, looked out of the contest at 76/6 during their chase. But Zane Green and Alexander Volschenk produced a breathtaking 109-run seventh-wicket partnership off just 49 balls to put Namibia within touching distance of another remarkable victory.Zimbabwe eventually held on, with Brad Evans delivering the decisive final over to seal a result that looked highly unlikely midway through the chase.Asked to bat first, Zimbabwe made an aggressive start through Ben Curran and Brian Bennett, who put on 64 for the opening wicket. Namibia struck with the final ball of the Powerplay when Bennett top-edged a pull off JJ Smit to deep midwicket for 32 off 21 balls.Dion Myers fell to Bernard Scholtz in the following over, before Gerhard Erasmus produced the biggest breakthrough by dismissing Sikandar Raza for a golden duck.Curran was then removed in the ninth over, and Erasmus struck again soon after to send back Wesley Madhavere.Zimbabwe had slumped to 79/5 in the 10th over and were in danger of being bowled out cheaply. But Ryan Burl and Brad Evans turned the innings around with a crucial 94-run partnership off 48 balls.Namibia's decision to return to spin for the final over proved particularly expensive. Burl smashed Erasmus for a six and three consecutive fours, taking 20 from the over as Zimbabwe surged to 195/6.Namibia's chase began with early pressure from Zimbabwe. Louren Steenkamp was dismissed by Blessing Muzarabani in the third over, while Erasmus made 12 before falling to Brad Evans.Loftie-Eaton briefly counterattacked with 20 off 13, but Brian Bennett then struck twice in three balls to leave Namibia at 66/4. Frylinck's 22 off 29 was unable to halt the slide, and when Ruben Trumpelmann fell to Sikandar Raza, Namibia were reeling at 76/6.Then came the extraordinary recovery.Volschenk attacked the bowling from the outset, hitting Wellington Masakadza for two sixes in the 13th over. Green joined him, and the pair combined power with sharp running to keep Namibia's hopes alive.Their partnership raced past 100, leaving Namibia needing only 16 from the final over with four wickets still in hand.Evans began the last over with a no-ball, but Namibia could take only two runs from it. Green was then run out for 54 off 26 after being caught short at the non-striker's end by a direct hit from Raza.Volschenk kept Namibia alive with a boundary but was dismissed for 56 off 29 when he edged a full, wide delivery, with wicketkeeper Tadiwanashe Marumani taking a superb one-handed catch.With two balls remaining, Namibia needed nine. Scholtz was run out attempting a desperate single before Evans held his nerve to bowl Jack Brassell for a duck and complete Zimbabwe's five-run victory.
Article Summary: Namibia looked out of the contest at 76/6 during their chase. Zane Green and Alexander Volschenk produced a breathtaking 109-run seventh-wicket partnership. Zimbabwe eventually held on, with Brad Evans delivering the decisive final over to seal a result that looked highly unlikely midway through the chase.

Article Title: Women’s Asia Cup: Sobhana Mostary recalls the India win that ‘changed everything’ for Bangladesh
Article Text:
Bangladesh's Sobhana Mostary (AP Photo)

From a village academy to international cricket

‘Day by day, I improve’

Harmanpreet Kaur : The childhood idol

A session with Laura Wolvaardt

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Cricket over medicine

The 2026 Women’s Asia Cup is already underway and Bangladesh enter the tournament with a familiar opportunity - to test themselves against the best in Asia and, potentially, India.For Sobhana Mostary, however, the Asia Cup carries a significance that goes well beyond the matches ahead. Six years after Bangladesh’s historic triumph in 2018, the memories of that campaign remain deeply connected to how she views the tournament and the growth of women’s cricket in her country.Bangladesh women's cricket has come a long way since its historic victory over India in the 2018 Women's Asia Cup, a victory that Sobhana Mostary believes transformed the nature of the sport in her country.For Mostary, the 2018 triumph remains a defining moment for Bangladesh women's cricket.“After 2018, we beat India and won the Asia Cup, so it was a huge change in Bangladesh women's cricket. Everything changed. They started giving us lots of facilities, money, everything. There was a lot of change,” Mostary told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interaction ahead of the Women’s Asia Cup 2026.In their 2018 campaign, Bangladesh beat India twice in the tournament, including a seven-wicket win in the group stage, before defeating the defending champions by three wickets in a thrilling final in Kuala Lumpur to win their maiden Women's Asia Cup title.The final went down to the last ball, with Jahanara Alam completing the winning two runs as Bangladesh chased down India's 112/9.The impact was immediate. Bangladesh Cricket Board announced a Bangladeshi Taka 2 crore reward for the victorious women's team. For Mostary, the legacy of that victory remains relevant even years later.“We think this Asia Cup, we fight for the title, because if we beat India, so maybe we own the Asia Cup,” she said.Now, as Bangladesh prepare for another Asia Cup campaign, Mostary knows the challenge is different. Bangladesh are in Group B alongside Sri Lanka, Indonesia and the UAE, while India are in Group A with Pakistan, Thailand and Hong Kong. A meeting between the two sides can only come in the knockout stage.Mostary's own journey began far away from the international spotlight. She started playing several sports as a child, including football, badminton and cricket. At the age of 10, her father took her to a cricket academy in her village. After around six months of training, she attended a trial conducted by the Bangladesh Krira Shiksha Pratisthan (BKSP) and was selected.That selection changed the course of her life. Mostary moved to Dhaka without her parents to pursue cricket. Her international debut came remarkably early. She was just 16 years old when she first played for Bangladesh.But making her debut did not immediately translate into a regular place in the XI. Mostary recalled spending the next three to three-and-a-half years travelling with the Bangladesh team without getting consistent opportunities to play.“It was very difficult. I always travelled with the team, but couldn't play. I just waited and thought that someday the opportunity would come and I could show my strength, ” she said.The patience eventually began to pay off. The ICC described Mostary as a bright future prospect in 2023, but the batter believes she is still working towards fulfilling that potential.“I don't think I have fulfilled my dream and that bright future yet, but day by day, I improve, ” she said.Interestingly, one of Mostary's biggest inspirations comes from across the border. Her childhood idol is Harmanpreet Kaur, the India captain whose batting left a lasting impression on her as a young cricketer from Bangladesh. Mostary specifically recalled watching Harmanpreet's memorable 2017 Women's World Cup innings against Australia, when the Indian batter smashed an unbeaten 171.“That match inspired me a lot, I followed her batting, everything how she controls the match, and now the time how she captains. I just followed everything, ” Mostary admitted.Playing India, in fact, remains something she describes as exciting rather than intimidating.“For Bangladeshi fans, playing India is a very good match. They are crazy fans and lots of supporters come to watch. It is a normal match, but normally playing India is very interesting and always very exciting for us,” she added.Mostary also has a particular appreciation for India's bowling attack. Asked which Indian bowler she would like to face, she picked Deepti Sharma, praising the all-rounder's consistency and variety.“Deepti Sharma is always the top bowler in the Indian side, she has played consistently for so many years and improved day by day. I love her bowling, ” Mostary said.While Harmanpreet remains her childhood idol, Mostary has another player she would love to train with, South Africa captain Laura Wolvaardt.“I want to practise with Laura Wolvaardt, I really like her batting, and she's also a good human being,” she said.There was a time when cricket was not even Mostary's first career choice. Asked what she might have done had she not pursued cricket, she revealed that becoming a doctor was a possibility.“Maybe a doctor, because my mother wanted me to be a doctor,” she said.Instead, the 16-year-old who once left home to pursue cricket has now spent years representing Bangladesh on the international stage.“I struggled for three or four years, but now I have improved,” she said.And with India once again standing in Bangladesh's path, Mostary knows exactly what another victory could mean.(Watch DP World Women's Asia live on Sony Sports Ten 1 SD & HD & Sony LIV.)
Article Summary: Bangladesh women's cricket has come a long way since its historic victory over India in the 2018 Women's Asia Cup. Sobhana Mostary believes the victory transformed the nature of the sport in her country. Mostary's childhood idol is Harmanpreet Kaur, whose batting left a lasting impression on her.

Article Title: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi makes a statement! Teenager misses ton as East Zone match Central Zone’s first-innings total
Article Text:

Brief scores: Central Zone 266 & 45/3 in 20 overs (Mukesh Kumar 2-14) vs East Zone 266 all out in 57 overs (Abhimanyu Easwaran 69, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi 92; Aryan Pandey 3-43, Yash Thakur 3-66, Harsh Dubey 4-66).

BENGALURU: In 118 minutes and 81 balls, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi offered a glimpse of the raw talent that has made him one of Indian cricket ’s most sought-after prospects. The southpaw backs his big-hitting ability irrespective of the format and his fearless approach was on full display as the East Zone opener smashed 92 (7x4, 7x6) against Central Zone on Day 2 of their Duleep Trophy semifinal at the BCCI Centre of Excellence here on Monday.At 15 years and 157 days, Sooryavanshi became the youngest player to score a 50 in the tournament, breaking Central Zone’s Laxman Singh’s record of 16 years and 23 days, set in January 1969.The innings was more than just a record. Since his Ranji Trophy debut in 2024, the teenager had managed 215 runs from nine first-class matches. While he has built strong credentials in white-ball cricket, the longer format remains a stern test. Sooryavanshi was in no mood to let a red-ball challenge pass without making a statement.The first session was all about his attacking display. After getting off the mark with a risky single, the left-hander struck his first boundary with a stylish square drive. That was merely an appetiser, as he repeatedly looked to score in the V against the pacers, including Yash Thakur, whom he deposited over the bowler’s head for his first six.His 18 singles were as much a sign of maturity as his seven sixes were of his power.His domination helped East Zone race to 64 in the first 10 overs. On 40, Sooryavanshi was handed a reprieve when Yash Rathod dropped a straightforward catch off Saransh Jain. The batter made the most of it, bringing up his half-century off 42 balls with a six over long-on.What stood out was not just the power, but the range. One particular assault on pacer Aryan Pandey was striking. Charging down the track, Sooryavanshi smashed the ball straight back over the bowler’s head for his fourth six.Such was his command that it seemed to matter little who was bowling. Off-spinner Saransh Jain, who recently made his India Test debut, was dealt with equal confidence, conceding a four and a six as Sooryavanshi raced towards the nervous nineties in the 25th over.However, he was left distraught when another attempt at a maximum landed in Arshad Khan’s hands at deep mid-wicket off Harsh Dubey, leaving him eight runs short of his maiden first-class hundred.Along with Abhimanyu Easwaran’s 69, Sooryavanshi’s 92 formed the backbone of a 161-run opening stand that helped East Zone reach 266, exactly matching Central Zone’s first-innings total. Central were 45/3 at stumps.
Article Summary: East Zone opener smashed 92 (7x4, 7x6) against Central Zone on Day 2 of their Duleep Trophy semifinal at the BCCI Centre of Excellence here on Monday. At 15 years and 157 days, Sooryavanshi became the youngest player to score a 50 in the tournament.

Article Text:

From a village in Tripura to Commonwealth Games glory

CM urges Asmita to target Asian Games success

NEW DELHI: Tripura chief minister Manik Saha has fulfilled a promise made to Commonwealth Games gold medallist Asmita Dey, with the state government allotting her a piece of land in Agartala to build a house.The 23-year-old judoka was honoured in Tripura on Wednesday after becoming the first Indian judoka to win a Commonwealth Games gold medal.Dey won the women’s -48kg title in Glasgow after defeating Canada’s Heidi Quach in a dramatic golden-score contest. The state government also presented her with a cheque of Rs 10 lakh as part of the felicitation.Speaking at the event, Saha highlighted Dey’s difficult journey from a small village in South Tripura to the top of the Commonwealth Games podium. Her father, he noted, worked as a cycle mechanic in Sonaichari.“The journey from an obscure village in South Tripura to a podium finish at Glasgow was a race against time. Her father was a cycle mechanic at Sonaichari. Against all odds, she stood firm on her mission and achieved phenomenal success for the country,” he said.The chief minister recalled meeting Dey at Tripura Bhavan in New Delhi after her return from the Games.During that meeting, the judoka had expressed her wish to have a house in Agartala.“During the meeting, Asmita revealed she desperately wanted a house in Agartala. I promised to fulfil her wish, and today a piece of land has been allotted to her,” he said.Saha said Dey’s achievement could motivate more young athletes from Tripura to pursue sport at the highest level. He also urged her to remain disciplined as she prepares for the Asian Games, particularly because of the strict anti-doping requirements.“I urge Asmita to remain alert, particularly about food, because she has to pass through a stringent dope test before joining the prestigious Asian Games. We believe she will shine again in the Asian Games by winning a medal for the country,” he said.Youth Affairs and Sports Minister Tinku Roy, Agartala Mayor Dipak Majumder and Arjuna award-winning gymnast Dipa Karmakar were among those who attended the felicitation ceremony.
Article Summary: Tripura chief minister Manik Saha has fulfilled a promise made to Commonwealth Games gold medallist Asmita Dey. The state government allotting her a piece of land in Agartala to build a house. The 23-year-old judoka was honoured in Tripura on Wednesday after becoming the first Indian judoka to win a Commonwealth games gold medal.

NEW DELHI: Somewhere on a muddy school field in Haryana right now, a teenager is perhaps drilling the same throwing technique over and over, just as she had watched on television just days ago. Her sole aim is to pull off the one like Sharmila Dhankar, India's Commonwealth Games shot put gold medallist.Before the 2026 CWG campaign, she, like many of us, had almost certainly never heard the name. And it's not because Dhankar had not won anything before the Glasgow Games; she had, a gold medal in the Women's Shot Put F57 event at the 2026 Fazza International Para Athletics Championship, but because one of the primary institutions whose entire job was to carry that story back from the medal podium to villages and training grounds across the state has, for all practical purposes, gone quiet.That's the part of this story that rarely gets told. India walked away from Glasgow with 39 medals, and for a week, the athletes who won them were everywhere, garlanded at airports, seated beside ministers, their faces on the evening news. But medals don't build the next generation of athletes by themselves. Somebody has to keep telling their stories, long after the felicitation photo is filed away, to the kid training in a dusty school ground who needs proof that this path actually leads somewhere.We wanted to know which state sports departments are still doing their job of promoting the sports and their grassroots on their social media platforms, and which ones seem to have simply logged off. So we scrolled through the timelines ourselves. Here's what we found.No state produced more glory in Glasgow than Haryana. Eleven medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze, spanning boxing, wrestling, athletics, and para sport, headlined by a Neeraj Chopra silver that will be replayed on sports channels for years.Alongside him were names most of India still had little knowledge of. The likes of Preeti Pawar, Jaismine Lamboria, Sakshi Chaudhary, Priya Ghanghas, Sachin Siwach, and Ankush Panghal, all of whom trained in government facilities, under government schemes, and who'd probably appreciate their own state department cheering as loudly for them as it does for its concert lineups.Because that's the thing. The Sports Department, Government of Haryana's X account has posted exactly once in all of 2026, and it's a flyer for the music acts playing at the Chief Minister's Cup.Facebook and Instagram follow a similar rhythm with a short cluster of posts around that February event, and then not much else.Eleven medals, and not one dedicated post to show for it. Somewhere in Rohtak or Bhiwani, a young pugilist training in Priya Ghanghas's discipline would probably just like a little proof that someone up top is paying attention.Manipur's page has an odd time-capsule quality to it. This is the state that gave India Mirabai Chanu, one of the country's most beloved Olympic medalists, and this Commonwealth Games alone produced four medalists from Manipur, Chanu's gold among them, alongside Rishikanta Singh, Bindyarani Devi, and Jadumani Singh.And yet the Department of Youth Affairs & Sports' X account hasn't posted since October 2023, a "Run for Unity" event, frozen well before any of this year's medals happened.Although the Facebook page has had a few sporadic posts here and there this year, its Instagram account has managed just two posts since January. It’s the kind of gap that makes you wonder if someone simply forgot the login details somewhere along the way.If there's one number in this whole exercise worth sitting with, it's this: the official Sports Department, Government of Rajasthan hasn't posted on Facebook since April 14, 2012.Fourteen years, through Arundhati Choudhary's Commonwealth gold and everything else that's happened in Rajasthan sport since.Its X account's last original post predates a retweet from March 2021, and there's no Instagram at all. A parallel handle, the Rajasthan State Sports Council, exists across all three platforms and is barely livelier.Somewhere behind Choudhary's medal is a genuinely good story, but it just hasn't found a home on the one page built to tell it.Gulveer Singh managed both a silver and a bronze for Uttar Pradesh this Games, a rare double that would make a great centrepiece for the state's sporting year. Instead, across two separate official handles on three platforms, Uttar Pradesh Sports has produced little beyond reposts, while its sister account, Sports Directorate, Govt of Uttar Pradesh, hasn't posted at all in 2026.Delhi Government, for its part, doesn't run a dedicated sports account at all on any of the popular social media platforms, so gold medalist Harsh Singh and bronze medalist Tejaswin Shankar, both representing India's capital, don't really have an institutional cheerleader online, their wins quietly absorbed into the general churn of city government updates. Both athletes are, in effect, doing their own promotional legwork.Set against all that quiet, Tamil Nadu feels like a different sport altogether. Its Sports Tamil Nadu handles post multiple times a day, celebrating not just its own three medalists, Praveen Chithravel, Selva Prabhu, Muthupandi Raja, but athletes from other states too, weaving in government scheme updates without it ever reading like bureaucracy.Every medallist got a dedicated post. Somewhere in Tamil Nadu, a kid training in long jump or wrestling doesn't have to wonder whether the sport leads anywhere. The state tells them, publicly, almost daily.Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka's Facebook and Instagram pages, Assam, Bihar, and Tripura all follow a version of that same habit, active, consistent, generous with attention toward athletes nobody outside their district would otherwise know existed.Kerala doesn't run a separate sports handle on X but keeps its Facebook and Instagram genuinely lively, making sure Murali Sreeshankar and Mohammed Basil's silvers got their due.Andhra Pradesh mirrors that same rhythm across all three platforms.Not every state falls neatly into being inactive or staying proactive. Punjab's account managed just two posts on X all year, New Year's and Republic Day, though its Facebook and Instagram carry a bit more life around coaching and departmental meetings, even if athletes rarely get top billing.Uttarakhand was genuinely active last year before cooling off in 2026, leaning more toward government scheme announcements on Facebook, though its Instagram at least carried two posts around the Games.Maharashtra has dedicated posts up for both Sarvesh Kushare and Dilip Gavit, with Instagram staying fairly regular, enough effort to stay out of the quiet column.Karnataka's X account hasn't posted since March 2024, around an unrelated cultural-team event, even though its Facebook and Instagram have stayed warm and active toward its CWG medalists.It is worth asking why this actually matters, beyond good manners. Well, a state sports department's social media feed isn't just a courtesy board for congratulations; it's one of the cheapest, most direct tools available to build the next generation of athletes.A youngster in a small town is far more likely to pick up a javelin because they saw a state government post celebrating someone from their own district. Even when it comes to promoting any government policy, social media can be as effective.Visibility drives aspiration. There's a funding logic too. Sponsors, corporates, and even state finance departments allocate resources partly based on visible public interest, and a well-run social account is often the easiest evidence a sport has that interest.ALSO READ: Anahat Singh: What is in the name? A word from Guru Nanak's prayer, now India's squash sensation Silence, on the other hand, sends the message that grassroots sport isn't a priority worth the effort of a single post, even when the state has just produced a medallist on the world stage.It is worth it because sometimes, the first step towards building a sporting culture is simply showing people that their achievements are being seen.
Article Summary: India won 39 medals at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Haryana produced 11 medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze. But the state sports department has posted just once in all of 2026. What do you think is more important for grassroots sports promotion? Government funding or social media presence? Share your view.

Article Title: ‘That video was not ordinary’: PM Modi praises Lovlina for objecting to distorted India map - Watch
Article Text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi shares a light moment with boxer Lovlina Borgohain. (PTI Photo)

‘That video was not ordinary’

Mirabai opens up about four difficult years

Narender's joke leaves Modi laughing

NEW DELHI: Boxer Lovlina Borgohain's decision to object to a distorted Indian map during the Commonwealth Games earned special appreciation from Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who described the moment as one that would be remembered for a long time.Lovlina, who won silver in the women's 75kg category in Glasgow, was among India's medal winners who interacted with Modi at his residence on Sunday. The meeting, attended by Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya, Minister of State for Sports Raksha Khadse and Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha, saw athletes recount their experiences from the Games in an informal and emotional setting.In a little over 10-minute video of the interaction shared by the Prime Minister's Office on Monday, Modi brought up Lovlina's confrontation with a restaurant in Glasgow after she noticed a distorted Indian map.“Kya hua wo restaurant waale se jhagda kar rahi thi? (What happened, you were fighting with that restaurant guy?)” Modi asked.Lovlina laughed before explaining why she intervened.“We had such a good performance and it was the last day of the Games. It was a happy occasion sir, we were celebrating and I didn't like it when I saw the distorted map. I politely told them and they have made the changes also,” she explained.Modi applauded the boxer for noticing the issue despite being in the middle of celebrations after her medal-winning campaign.“To be able to recognise the significance of that map at a time when you were celebrating and the Games were over, I can tell you truthfully, that video was not ordinary. It will be remembered by people for a very long time,” he told the Tokyo Olympics bronze medallist.India finished fourth in Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 golds, with boxing contributing seven gold medals.The interaction also provided an emotional window into Mirabai Chanu's journey to her gold medal in the women's 48kg category. The weightlifter produced a Games-record lift of 190kg, but her triumph came after four difficult years following her one-kilogram miss at the Paris Olympics. Modi asked Mirabai about the tears she shed on the podium and even fed her a laddu during their interaction.“Itne aansu tapak rahe the (So many tears were rolling down),” Modi remarked.Mirabai explained that the tears represented years of accumulated emotions.“I was very happy and emotional at that moment. I was crying because I missed a medal in the Paris Olympics by one kilogram. I have faced a lot in these last four years. I was battling injuries and some family problems too.“There were a lot of things. So, these four years were very tough for me. And when I stood on the podium, our flag went up and the anthem played, it was hard to stop myself,” she said.The meeting also had its lighter moments. Boxer Narender Berwal, who won silver in the +90kg category, recalled a funny exchange with a Pakistani boxer after beating him at the 2015 World Military Games.“During the 2015 World Military Games, I had a bout with a Pakistani boxer. I won it but when we were together in the medical room for treatment to our niggles, he said to me 'Bhaijan aapka naam Narender hai, aapke coach ka naam Narender hai, aapke Pradhan Mantri ka naam Narender hai, mujhe Narender naam se nafrat ho gayi hai.' (Brother, you, your coach and your PM are all named Narender. I hate this name now),” he recalled, drawing laughter from Modi.The Prime Minister also underlined the broader significance of the athletes' achievements, saying their medals were helping inspire a new generation.“I have been in this house for 12-13 years now and if there is one group that I have met regularly here, it is the athletes because of your efforts to win medals for India and your tradition of scaling new heights.“Far more than our push to promote sports in schools, it is your medals that inspire people,” Modi said.
Article Summary: Lovlina Borgohain won silver in the women's 75kg category in Glasgow. Prime Minister Narendra Modi described the moment as one that would be remembered for a long time. India finished fourth in Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 golds, with boxing contributing seven gold medals.

Article Title: ‘From every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping’: PM Modi’s heartfelt message to CWG heroes - Watch
Article Text:
PM Narendra Modi interacted with India's CWG 2026 medal winners at his residence on Sunday. (Pic credit: PM Modi's X post)

Mirabai recalls four years of struggle

‘One family will bring three medals’

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India’s Glasgow success

NEW DELHI: “From every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping.”Prime Minister Narendra Modi had an emotional message for Mirabai Chanu as he interacted with India's Commonwealth Games 2026 medal winners at his residence on Sunday, reflecting on the sacrifices behind the country's successful campaign in Glasgow.Modi hosted the medal-winning contingent at 7, Lok Kalyan Marg and heard athletes recount some of the moments that defined their journeys at the Games. India returned from Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze, finishing fourth in the overall standings.During one of the conversations, Modi recalled the emotional scenes surrounding Mirabai's gold-medal triumph.“Tears were falling from you. I feel as if from every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping,” Modi told the Olympic silver medallist.Mirabai, who won gold in Glasgow, opened up about the difficult journey that preceded her Commonwealth Games triumph, including the disappointment of the Paris Olympics.“I was very happy, and emotional too. That day the happiness was greater and I cried because at the Paris Olympics, I lost a medal by 1 kg. In a player’s life what all we have to face. So within these 4 years, how much and what all I had faced, every time injuries were going on and all that was happening.So with great difficulty I had faced these 4 years. So when all that happened, on the podium when I stood, sir, and when our flag goes up and our national anthem plays, sir, we cannot stop, sir, tears come out on their own,” she said.Modi responded by highlighting the wider impact of the athletes' achievements.“This is very good. It is not as if this achievement of yours is considered only your achievement; your victory becomes a very big inspiration for the coming generations.”The informal interaction also saw athletes share lighter and deeply personal moments from their Glasgow campaigns.Modi reminded para shot put gold medallist Sharmila Dhankar of a promise she had made earlier.“You made a promise. Last time, yours, both daughters will become players,” Modi said with a smile.Dhankar replied: “Haanji, right now they are young in age. In the next Commonwealth, one family will bring 3 medals.”Men's 100m T47 gold medallist Dilip Gavit, meanwhile, spoke about dedicating his performance to his guru.“When I was running, when my event was on 29th (July), that day was Guru Purnima, so that day I gave a gift to my guru,” he was heard saying in the video.In another video posted by Modi, gold medallist boxer Sakshi Chaudhary introduced herself and the contingent.“Hello friends! This is Sakshi Chaudhary. Today, our honourable Prime Minister has invited us, the Commonwealth Games medalists, and we feel very proud. We are extremely happy to have met him; he is very humble. Sir, would you like to say something?” she said.Modi replied with a message that summed up his interaction with the athletes: “Jo khelega, woh khilega” (The one who plays, will blossom). “Always cheer for Bharat.”India's fourth-place finish came despite a significantly smaller contingent and a reduced sporting programme compared to Birmingham 2022. India sent 122 athletes to Glasgow, compared to 210 in Birmingham, while 30 of its 61 medals in 2022 came in sports that were not part of the Glasgow programme.Despite those limitations, India retained its fourth-place position and improved its medal conversion rate, with 38 athletes returning home with medals. Long-distance runner Gulveer Singh was the only Indian athlete to win two medals.The Glasgow Games concluded after 11 days, with Scotland handing over the Commonwealth Games flag and ceremonial baton to India ahead of the 2030 edition in Ahmedabad.The symbols were handed to Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra, Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha and Gujarat Deputy Chief Minister Harsh Sanghavi during the closing ceremony.Ahmedabad will become only the second Indian city to host the Commonwealth Games after New Delhi staged the 2010 edition.
Article Summary: PM Narendra Modi hosted medal-winning contingent at 7, Lok Kalyan Marg. Modi heard athletes recount some of the moments that defined their journeys. India returned from Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze.
